titre: Spindletop, 1901: A Salt Dome Launches the Oil Age
accroche: On January 10, 1901, a Texas well blasts oil 50 meters into the air. Underneath: a hidden hill of salt that put crude within drilling reach.
contenu_vulgarise:
On January 10, 1901, near Beaumont, Texas, a well reaches a depth of 347 meters and suddenly starts gushing. The jet, nicknamed the Lucas Gusher, shoots more than 150 feet (about 50 meters) into the air and flows at roughly 100,000 barrels a day, an unheard-of figure for the time. It takes nine days to bring the well under control.

## A hill that is nothing like a hill

Before 1901, a former Beaumont brickmaker, Pattillo Higgins, insists there is oil beneath a small rise called Spindletop. He has no geological training and struggles to convince anyone, until he teams up with Captain Anthony F. Lucas, a mining engineer who had observed the link between salt, sulfur, gas, and oil while working the salt domes of Louisiana. Lucas drills despite unfavorable reports, runs out of money at 575 feet, then finds new backers, including banker Andrew Mellon, to keep going.

## Why salt attracts oil

Spindletop sits on a layer of Jurassic salt, buried under younger sediments. Salt is ductile: under the uneven load of the layers above it, it slowly flows upward, in a column, over millions of years. As it pierces the overlying layers, it deforms and bends them upward on contact, forming a dome. Salt itself is nearly impermeable: it acts as a lid. Oil and gas, lighter than the water soaking the porous rock around them, migrate and collect against this lid, in the layers bent by the dome. A hill of salt invisible at the surface thus becomes an oil trap underground. The USGS lists 263 known or suspected salt domes in this one region of the Gulf of Mexico alone.

## What Spindletop changed

Within six months, thirteen wells are gushing on the same dome; by the end of 1902, the field counts two hundred and eighty-five. The price of oil collapses locally, but the sudden supply of cheap crude feeds the nascent automobile industry and turns Texas into an oil state. The financing raised for Lucas gives rise to companies that will become Texaco and Gulf Oil. And the method repeats: spotting a salt dome now means looking for an oil trap, from Louisiana to the Gulf of Mexico. A mineral rise nobody had thought to drill becomes, within a decade, the treasure map of an entire industry.

repere.texte: On January 10, 1901, Anthony F. Lucas's well reaches a depth of 347 meters at Spindletop, Texas, and gushes more than 150 feet (50 m) high, at an estimated rate of 100,000 barrels a day. Thirteen wells gush on the same salt dome within six months; 285 wells are operating there by the end of 1902. carte.punch: A hidden hill of salt turned Texas into an oil state within six months.
carte.idee: On January 10, 1901, a well drilled on the Spindletop salt dome (Texas) gushes 50 meters high and flows at 100,000 barrels a day. The ductile salt pierces the sedimentary layers and bends them into an impermeable dome: a perfect trap for the oil migrating and collecting beneath it.

quiz.question: Why does a salt dome form an oil trap?
choix: Salt chemically attracts oil molecules dissolved in the surrounding water
Salt, ductile and impermeable, bends the layers as it rises and blocks the oil migrating beneath it
Oil forms directly from salt under the pressure of the overlying layers
Salt cools the surrounding rock, which condenses the oil present nearby
quiz.explication: Salt flows slowly upward under the uneven load of the sediments, deforms and bends the layers it pierces, then acts as an impermeable lid: oil and gas, lighter than water, collect against it. None of the other proposals describe any real mechanism.
